caseName: Victoria's Secret Stores, LLC v. Herald Sq. Owner LLC
court: Supreme Court of New York, New York County, Commercial Division; affirmed by the Appellate Division, First Department
keyFacts: Victoria's Secret's retail/office tenancy at 2 Herald Square continued after the landlord terminated the lease for nonpayment during the COVID-19 pandemic; the tenant argued the pandemic excused performance and refused to vacate or pay post-termination amounts.
outcome: The landlord was granted summary judgment enforcing Article 21(A) of the lease, which fixed holdover rent at three times the rent otherwise payable; the trial court calculated additional holdover damages of $17,589,819.91 for the retail portion and $2,331,106.71 for the office portion, and the First Department affirmed treble-rent holdover damages as an enforceable liquidated-damages provision.
dollarAmountBasis: Sum of trial court's additional holdover-damages calculation for the retail ($17,589,819.91) and office ($2,331,106.71) portions of the lease under the 3x-rent holdover clause; later payments/partial satisfactions in the litigation are not netted out of this figure
notes: This litigation had multiple stages and partial-payment amounts (e.g., a later 'Office Judgment Amount' after tenant payments); the figure here reflects the initial summary-judgment holdover-damages calculation under the lease's treble-rent clause, not a single final net judgment number. Verify current docket status before citing an exact final collected amount.

caseName: ESRT 501 Seventh Ave., LLC v. Regine, Ltd.
citation: Appeal Nos. 16109, 16109A, Index No. 655960/20 (App. Div., 1st Dep't, June 9, 2022)
court: Supreme Court of New York, Appellate Division, First Department
keyFacts: Retail clothing tenant Regine, Ltd. remained in possession of Midtown Manhattan store space at 501 Seventh Avenue past its June 2020 lease-end date and did not pay post-expiration rent.
outcome: The Appellate Division upheld the lease's holdover-rent provision requiring the tenant to pay 200% of its prior rent for the holdover period, treating it as an enforceable liquidated-damages clause rather than an unenforceable penalty.
notes: Total dollar figure for the holdover rent recovered was not confirmed in the sources reviewed; the 200%-of-rent multiplier is confirmed.

citation: 108 Cal. App. 5th 666 (Cal. Ct. App., 1st Dist., Div. 5, 2025)
court: California Court of Appeal, First Appellate District, Division Five
keyFacts: Commercial landlord Baca leased space in Fremont, California to tenant Kuang and served a 30-day notice terminating the tenancy; several days after the notice period expired (with rent current), Kuang tendered a rent check that Baca deposited without objection. The lease contained a standard clause doubling rent for any holdover.
outcome: The trial court had ruled for the landlord, finding no consent to continued tenancy. The Court of Appeal reversed, holding the landlord's unconditional acceptance and deposit of the post-termination rent check created a presumption of a new month-to-month tenancy that the landlord failed to rebut, defeating the double-rent holdover claim.
notes: Useful as a 'holdover claim denied' precedent — illustrates the risk to landlords of accepting rent after a termination notice.

court: Florida District Court of Appeal, Second District
keyFacts: An auto dealership tenant failed to vacate leased premises at the end of its lease term. The landlords sued for double rent covering the entire holdover period plus special damages, and the trial court awarded damages directly to the landlords' principal stockholder.
outcome: The Court of Appeal reversed, holding Florida's statutory double-rent remedy is a penalty the landlord must affirmatively invoke by demand, and cannot be recovered retroactively for the holdover period preceding that demand; it also held damages belonging to a corporation cannot be awarded directly to an individual shareholder.
notes: Illustrates an important limitation on double-rent recovery: it is not automatic and does not reach back before the landlord's demand.

keyFacts: A successor property owner sued a commercial tenant for possession and back rent after the lease term expired; the tenant contended it had validly exercised a purchase option and therefore had a right to remain in possession.
outcome: The Appellate Court affirmed denial of the landlord's double-rent claim under Illinois's holdover statute (735 ILCS 5/9-202), holding that the tenant's good-faith, colorable claim of a right to occupy defeated the 'willful holdover' element the statute requires for the double-rent penalty.
notes: A denial case; shows that Illinois's holdover multiplier requires proof of willfulness/bad faith, not mere overstay.

court: Washington Court of Appeals, Division Three
keyFacts: Commercial unlawful-detainer action following a tenant's holdover past lease expiration; dispute concerned the scope of rent to be doubled under Washington's unlawful-detainer statute.
outcome: The court held RCW 59.12.170 requires courts to double all unpaid rent in a commercial unlawful-detainer judgment, whether the rent accrued before or during the unlawful-detainer period — establishing that the doubling is mandatory, not discretionary, in Washington commercial holdover cases.
notes: Older case but still cited as the controlling authority on RCW 59.12.170's mandatory-doubling rule in Washington commercial holdover matters.

citation: No. 03-11-00580-CV (Tex. App.—Austin, Third Court of Appeals, June 28, 2013, no pet.) (mem. op.)
court: Texas Court of Appeals, Third District (Austin)
keyFacts: A renegotiated commercial lease set base rent at $4,500/month and included a holdover clause doubling rent if the tenant failed to vacate at lease end. The tenant argued the doubled-rent holdover provision was an unenforceable penalty.
outcome: The trial court had granted the tenant summary judgment, ruling the double-rent holdover clause an unenforceable penalty. The Court of Appeals reversed, holding the doubled holdover rent was enforceable, contractually agreed-upon rent rather than a penalty.
dollarAmountBasis: Base rent was $4,500/month, doubling to $9,000/month during the holdover period, but no aggregate judgment figure was confirmed in sources reviewed
notes: Frequently cited in Texas commercial-leasing practice as confirming double-rent holdover clauses are enforceable, not per se penalties.

keyFacts: A commercial tenant in Monroeville, PA remained on leased business premises for about seven months after its two-year lease term expired, continuing to pay the same monthly rent, apparently with the landlord's acquiescence.
outcome: The Superior Court held the parties' post-expiration conduct evidenced formation of a new month-to-month tenancy rather than triggering the common-law rule that would have made the tenant liable for a full additional year (or an elevated holdover rate), because the landlord accepted continued occupancy and unchanged rent without objection.
notes: Illustrates how landlord acquiescence can defeat an elevated-rent holdover claim in Pennsylvania, similar in effect to Baca v. Kuang in California.

caseName: Rohrmoos Venture v. UTSW DVA Healthcare, LLP
keyFacts: A ground-lease dispute in which the tenant (UTSW) terminated the lease and successfully defended against the landlord's breach-of-contract counterclaim; UTSW then sought contractual attorney's fees as the prevailing party, supported largely by generalized attorney testimony placing fees between $800,000 and $1,000,000.
outcome: The Texas Supreme Court affirmed that UTSW was the prevailing party but reversed the attorney's-fee award for legally insufficient evidence, holding fee-shifting claimants must prove fees under the lodestar method (reasonable hours x reasonable rate, supported by contemporaneous billing records), not generalized testimony about a fee range; the case was remanded for a new fee determination.
dollarAmountBasis: Low end of the attorney's-fee range claimed and awarded at trial before the Supreme Court reversed for insufficient evidence
notes: Landmark case establishing Texas's modern lodestar proof requirements for contractual fee-shifting; frequently invoked in commercial lease litigation statewide.

caseName: Oak Park Investment Co. v. Lundy's, Inc.
keyFacts: A commercial lease contained a clause authorizing the recovery of reasonable attorney's fees upon breach; the trial court initially declined to award fees to the prevailing party.
outcome: The Court of Appeals held that an agreement in a commercial lease for recovery of reasonable attorney's fees is valid and enforceable under Kansas law.
notes: Foundational Kansas authority on enforceability of commercial-lease fee-shifting clauses; dollar figures for the fee award were not available in sources reviewed.

caseName: Wells & McElwee, P.C. v. Tiffany & Tomato, Inc. (companion appeals: Tiffany & Tomato, Inc. v. Wells & McElwee, P.C.)
keyFacts: A commercial lease of a roughly 154-year-old building in Athens, Georgia required the tenant to maintain and repair the roof and other improvements. The landlord (lessor) sued after the tenant (lessee) refused to repair the roof, and a jury awarded the landlord $45,667 in damages. Both sides then moved for contractual attorney's fees under the lease's fee-shifting clause.
outcome: The trial court granted the landlord's fee motion in part but denied the tenant's competing fee motion, rejecting the tenant's argument that it was the 'prevailing party' merely because the landlord had separately failed on a bad-faith fee claim under O.C.G.A. § 13-6-11; the Court of Appeals affirmed both rulings in companion appeals.
dollarAmountBasis: Underlying jury verdict on the landlord's breach-of-lease damages claim; the separate attorney's-fee dollar amounts were not confirmed in sources reviewed
notes: Good illustration that 'prevailing party' status for a lease fee clause is assessed relative to the parties' comparative success on the substantive claims, not any single sub-issue won.

caseName: 1046 Munras Properties, L.P. v. Kabod Coffee
keyFacts: A coffee-shop tenant leased retail space in a shopping center owned by 1046 Munras Properties and allegedly breached the lease's continuous-operation covenant. After prevailing, the landlord sought not only its underlying litigation fees but also 'fees on fees' — the fees incurred enforcing the fee-shifting provision itself and defending the appeal.
outcome: In Colorado's first published decision on the issue, the Court of Appeals held the lease and guaranty's broad fee-shifting language entitled the landlord to recover 'fees on fees,' reversing the portion of the trial court's ruling that had denied them.
notes: Notable for expanding, not limiting, fee recovery — a landlord-favorable outcome broadening what 'reasonable attorney's fees' clauses can capture.

caseName: RadioShack Corp. v. Cascade Crossing II, LLC
citation: 282 Ga. 841, 653 S.E.2d 680 (Ga. 2007) (answering a certified question from the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit)
keyFacts: RadioShack leased retail space in a shopping center under a lease with an exclusivity clause; after the landlord (Cascade Crossing II) leased to a competing merchant, RadioShack claimed a roughly $41,000 retroactive rent credit and paid reduced rent for years. The landlord sued for the agreed-upon back rent (~$172,039) and sought attorney's fees under the lease of roughly $280,000 in actual fees incurred.
outcome: The Georgia Supreme Court held that O.C.G.A. § 13-1-11 — a statute historically applied to promissory notes — also applies to commercial leases, capping recoverable attorney's fees at the statutory formula (15% of the first $500 collected plus 10% of the remainder) rather than the actual contractual fee amount, cutting the landlord's fee recovery to roughly $17,000–$17,288 instead of the ~$280,000 sought.
dollarAmountBasis: Actual attorney's fees the landlord sought under the lease's fee provision before the Georgia Supreme Court applied the O.C.G.A. § 13-1-11 statutory cap, which reduced recovery to roughly $17,000–$17,288
notes: A leading, cautionary Georgia case for commercial landlords: even an actual-fees clause in a lease can be statutorily capped well below fees actually incurred.

citation: 131 Cal. App. 4th 703, 32 Cal. Rptr. 3d 296 (Cal. Ct. App., 1st Dist., 2005)
court: California Court of Appeal, First Appellate District, Division Four
keyFacts: A commercial landlord terminated the tenant's lease for nonpayment and retained the tenant's substantial security deposit to offset the landlord's anticipated future-rent damages under Civil Code § 1951.2, rather than only damages accrued as of the statutory return date.
outcome: The Court of Appeal held Civil Code § 1950.7 unambiguously limits a commercial security deposit to covering unpaid rent and damages accrued as of the date the deposit is statutorily due back, and requires the landlord to calculate and return any 'excess.' The landlord's retention of the full deposit against speculative future-rent damages violated the statute.
notes: Frequently cited California authority for the proposition that a commercial security deposit cannot be applied to future/anticipated rent damages absent an express lease waiver of Civil Code § 1950.7.

caseName: Aljabban v. Fontana Indoor Swap Meet, Inc.
citation: 54 Cal. App. 5th 482 (Cal. Ct. App., 4th Dist., Div. 1, 2020) (unpublished; nonciteable under Cal. R. Ct. 8.1115)
court: California Court of Appeal, Fourth Appellate District, Division One
keyFacts: A husband-and-wife team operated a beauty salon on the premises of an indoor swap meet under a commercial lease with Fontana Indoor Swap Meet, Inc. (FISM). After the tenants vacated, FISM withheld $680 of the security deposit to cover repair costs.
outcome: The Court of Appeal held that, under Civil Code § 1950.7(c), a commercial landlord may apply a security deposit to repair costs only if the lease expressly authorizes that use; because this lease contained no such authorization, FISM's withholding of the $680 was improper.
dollarAmountBasis: Amount of the security deposit withheld for repairs that the court held was not authorized by the lease
notes: This is an unpublished California opinion; under Cal. R. Ct. 8.1115 it may not be cited as precedent in California courts. Included here only as an illustrative, real, verifiable fact pattern — not as binding authority. Flag this limitation to any user of the valuation tool.

caseName: Oak Forest Properties LLC v. RER Financial, Inc.
citation: 2018 IL App (1st) 161704-U (Ill. App. Ct., 1st Dist., Sept. 24, 2018) (unpublished Rule 23 order)
court: Appellate Court of Illinois, First District
keyFacts: A landlord and a tax-preparation franchisee entered a commercial lease for a strip-mall unit in Oak Forest, Illinois, with construction-delay and inspection disputes leading both sides to sue. The tenant counterclaimed for, among other things, return of its $3,403.60 security deposit.
outcome: After a two-week trial, the court ordered the security deposit returned to the tenant, but held the tenant did not achieve 'prevailing party' status for purposes of the lease's fee-shifting clause because the deposit's value was insignificant relative to the much larger, more complex breach-of-contract claims at issue; the Appellate Court affirmed.
dollarAmountBasis: Security deposit ordered returned to the tenant ($3,403.60, rounded)
notes: Illinois Rule 23 order — unpublished and of limited precedential value under Illinois court rules, but the facts and dollar figures are independently verifiable from the opinion text. Useful for showing that a small deposit-return win can be swamped by, and irrelevant to, the outcome of much larger contract claims in the same suit.

caseName: Urban Soccer Inc. v. Royal Wine Corp.
citation: 2016 N.Y. Slip Op. 26250 (Sup. Ct., N.Y. Cnty., Commercial Div. 2016)
court: Supreme Court of New York, New York County, Commercial Division
keyFacts: Royal Wine Corp. held a commercial security deposit belonging to Urban Soccer Inc. under a real-property rental agreement. Instead of maintaining the deposit at a bank branch located in New York as required by General Obligations Law § 7-103, Royal Wine deposited it at a Wells Fargo branch in New Jersey, even though New York branches were available.
outcome: The court found Royal Wine Corp. technically violated GOL § 7-103(2) by holding the deposit outside New York, but held this was a 'technical statutory violation' without fiduciary implications; because there was no commingling and Urban Soccer suffered no actual damages, the statute provided no remedy and the tenant was not entitled to relief.
notes: Important nuance case: a technical statutory violation regarding where a commercial deposit is held does not, by itself, entitle the tenant to damages absent commingling or actual harm.

keyFacts: Dispute over a commercial security deposit in Massachusetts, where the tenant argued the landlord was required to hold the deposit separately and pay interest on it, as is required for residential deposits.
outcome: The court held Massachusetts's residential security-deposit protections (segregation from the landlord's other funds and interest payment) do not extend to commercial tenancies; a commercial landlord may commingle a security deposit with its own funds and need not pay interest on it absent a contrary lease provision.
notes: A structural/negative-result case: shows that in Massachusetts (as in most states), the strong statutory deposit protections written for residential tenants generally do not apply to commercial tenants.
